title: Werk jij hier?
goal: Put the verb in the right place in Dutch statements and questions, drop the t after every verb when je/jij follows it, and say what is not so with niet.

content: It is Friday afternoon, the end of Sofia's first week at work, and the office has drinks. Everyone wants to ask the new colleague something. In this lesson you will learn where the verb goes in Dutch statements and questions, how to ask a question with every verb, and how to say “not” with

content.text: Friday afternoon. Sofia is still at her laptop. Daan comes to her desk.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Sofia, werk je nog? Het is borrel!

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Borrel? Hoe zeg je “borrel” in het Engels?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: “Drinks”. De borrel is heel Nederlands! Wat drink je?

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Wijn, graag. En jij? Drink jij ook wijn?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Nee, ik drink bier. Proost!

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Proost! Lekker!

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Ben je moe?

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Nee, ik ben niet moe. Ik ben blij!

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Super! En het werk? Is het werk moeilijk?

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Nee, het werk is niet moeilijk. Maar Nederlands is moeilijk!

words.meaning: drinks with colleagues or friends, an informal get-together (often on Friday afternoon)

words.note: het here is for the situation, like Hoe gaat het? (01-a).
words.example: Sofia, werk je nog? Het is borrel!

words.note: A fixed question. wat as a question word on its own comes in 04-b.
01-a used lekker in Slaap lekker!, a different use.
01-a's Niet zo goed. was a fixed chunk — this is the word itself.

props.translation: It's drinks time! What are you drinking? — Wine, please.
props.note: Repeats dialogue 1's opening lines.

props.translation: Are you drinking wine too? — No, I'm drinking beer. The colleague is drinking water.
props.note: jij right after the verb; the right fact instead of niet (as since 02-a).

content: Drink jij ook wijn? — Nee, ik drink bier. De collega drinkt water.

props.translation: Coffee? — No, thank you.
props.note: Nee, dank je. is the polite way to turn down an offer, next to Ja, graag! (02-b).

words.meaning: No, thank you (the polite answer to an offer)

content: : drinks together on Friday afternoon, around five, with beer, wine, soft drinks and snacks such as bitterballen (fried meat balls). You say “Proost!” and chat about the week — it is heel gezellig.
Dutch people also ask quite direct questions, like “Woon je alleen?” — that is friendly, not rude.

words.note: vrijdag = Friday, middag = afternoon; days of the week are taught later (09-a).

words.example: Woon je alleen? — Nee, ik woon bij Noor.

content: Three sentence types, three word orders. Statement:

blocks.content: In a Dutch statement the subject comes first, with the finite verb right behind it, so the verb is the second part of the sentence. The subject can be one word or several: Karin, het werk, de collega. Little words like ook, niet, een beetje and thuis come after the verb — never between the subject and the verb. Later lessons put other words first; the verb then still stays second.

props.translation: I work at an IT company.
props.note: Recycles werken bij (02-b).

props.translation: Daan drinks beer.
I also live in Utrecht.
props.note: ook comes right after the verb, never between the subject and the verb.

content: (jij before the verb keeps the t.)
In a yes/no question the finite verb comes first, then the subject, then the rest — now with every verb, not only zijn, komen, wonen and spreken.

props.translation: Do you work here? — Yes, I work here, at the office.
props.note: Verb first, then jij; the t drops. op kantoor = at the office (no article).

words.note: No article: op kantoor, not op het kantoor.

props.translation: Do you work here, sir? — Yes, I work here.
props.note: u always keeps the t.

content: hier, meneer? — Ja, ik werk hier.

props.translation: Are you reading a book in Dutch? — Yes!
props.note: jij after the verb: no t; z → s stays (lees).

content: een boek in het Nederlands? — Ja!
Dutch has no helper verb like English “do”:
After a question word, the verb comes right behind it, then the subject.

props.translation: Where do you work? — At an IT company.
Where do you live? — I live in the centre.
How is the work? — Good!
Who speaks French? — The colleague.
props.note: wie as the subject: the verb follows it directly and stays singular.

blocks.content: No t when je/jij follows the verb

content: comes right behind the verb, the verb is just the stem: werk je, woon jij, drink je, spreek je. After u, hij, zij or a name the stem keeps its t: werkt u, werkt hij, werkt Karin. And jij before the verb also keeps the t: jij werkt.
A stem that already ends in t keeps it:

props.translation: Are you still working? — No, I'm not working.
props.note: je right after the verb: no t. nog = still.

props.translation: Do you live in the centre? — No, I don't live in the centre. I live in Utrecht-Oost.
props.note: jij after the verb: no t. niet right before the place (a preview of the next section).

props.translation: Are you eating a sandwich?
props.note: The stem already ends in t, so no extra t — like hij heet (02-b).

props.translation: Are you studying psychology, Noor? — Yes, I'm studying psychology.
props.note: je right after the verb: no t.

content: psychologie, Noor? — Ja, ik studeer psychologie.

ie in niet, wie, bier is a short, clear “ee” as in English “see” — never like English “eye” or “pie”. Dutch w (werk, wie, wijn, water, woon) is softer than English w: let your top teeth touch your lower lip lightly, between an English v and w.

props.translation: Are you tired? — No, I'm not tired. I'm happy!
props.note: niet before the adjective moe. Questions put niet in the same places: Ben je niet moe? = Aren’t you tired?

props.translation: Where is Karin? — Karin isn't coming. She works at home, in Amersfoort.
props.note: komt niet: only a verb, so niet goes at the end. komen here means ‘to come’, a new use of komen (02-a taught komen uit).

props.translation: Is Utrecht-Oost far? — No, it's not far.
props.note: het here is for the distance, like Hoe gaat het?

props.translation: Do you live alone? — No, I live with Noor.
props.note: A direct but friendly question (culture note above). Nee + the right fact: bij Noor.

content: Woon je alleen? — Nee, ik woon

props.translation: He doesn't come from the Netherlands. He comes from Belgium. I don't live in Amsterdam.
props.note: niet before the place (uit + country, in + city), then the right fact. Recycles komen uit (02-a).

props.translation: Noor doesn't speak fast with me.
props.note: niet before snel, a word like an adjective here. met mij recycled from 01-a.

props.translation: Dutch isn't easy.
props.note: makkelijk is the opposite of moeilijk (03-a).

children.content: Ja, ik woon in het centrum.

content: Answering: Ja, … + the full sentence; Nee, … + the sentence with niet, or the right fact (as since 02-a), often both. In the answer, jij/je becomes ik and the verb changes back to the ik-form. To say “not a” or “no” + a noun (no wine, not a programmer), Dutch uses another word, which comes in lesson 04-b. For now, say what is true:

props.translation: Do you work here, sir? — Yes, I work here.
props.note: u → ik; short answers like Ja. and Nee hoor. are fine too.

content: Werkt u hier, meneer? — Ja, ik werk hier.

passage.title: Werk je nog?
passage.content:
Noor: Hoi Sofia! Werk je nog?
Sofia: Nee, ik werk niet. Het is borrel op kantoor!
Noor: Gezellig! Wat drink je?
Sofia: Wijn. Daan drinkt bier.
Noor: En Karin? Is Karin daar ook?
Sofia: Nee, Karin komt niet. Ze werkt thuis, in Amersfoort.
Noor: Spreek je Nederlands met Daan?
Sofia: Ja! Met Daan en met de collega uit België. Nederlands is niet makkelijk, maar het is gezellig!
Noor: Super! Ben je moe?
Sofia: Nee, ik ben niet moe. Ik ben heel blij!
Noor: Ik ben thuis. Tot straks!
Sofia: Tot straks!

data.instruction: You are at drinks with a new colleague. Write 2–4 short sentences: two questions (one yes/no question, one with waar, wie or hoe) and one or two sentences about yourself with niet.

items.prompt: You are at drinks with a new colleague. Write 2–4 short sentences: two questions (one yes/no question, one with waar, wie or hoe) and one or two sentences about yourself with niet.
authorsVersion: Werk jij ook thuis? Waar woon jij? Ik woon niet in het centrum. Ik woon in Utrecht-Oost.
items.note: Model answer by Sofia. Also fine with u: Werkt u …?; niet before a place, after the verb.

blocks.content: Statement: subject + verb + rest — the verb is second.
Yes/no question: verb first (Werk jij hier?). Question word + verb + subject (Waar woon je?).
je/jij after the verb: no t (werk je, drink jij); u, hij, zij keep it (werkt u); eet je keeps its stem t.
niet: at the end (Ik werk niet.), before an adjective (Ik ben niet moe.), before a place (Ik woon niet in Amsterdam.) — never between subject and verb.
Answer: Ja, … / Nee, … niet … / Nee, + the right fact.
